newsitem.title: UK: UK house price boom confined to London - analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK house price boom confined to London - analysts.

text.p: The belief that Britain is enjoying a nationwide housing boom is a myth, a growing number of economists now say.

Soaring London house prices, boosted by large City bonuses and an influx of Hong Kong Chinese to Britain ahead of the colony's return to China, have not spread much beyond the capital's boundaries and the health of the housing market outside is spotty.
"London's frothy prices are not spreading," Marsh said, "Prices in the South of England are only slightly stronger than in the North," according to Halifax spokesman Gary Marsh.

Simon Briscoe, UK economist at Nikko Securities, agreed. "Britain is enjoying an international boom in banking, financial services and tourism, but it is focused heavily on London with middle income groups feeling the benefit."

London house prices have grown by an average of 17 percent over the last year, but in England's southeast, a much bigger residential property region, prices have only risen by around nine percent, Halifax figures show.
In the less affluent North house prices have grown by between four and five percent.
A survey by the UK Land Registry published on Thursday echoed this portrait of a patchy housing market recovery.

It said that while house prices in some parts of London had shot up by as much as 27 percent during the last year, in parts of the north of England price rises had been as little as 1.7 percent in the same period.
"Large City bonuses and an influx of Hong Kong chinese snapping up property developments are behind London's robust house price growth", Marsh said.
He believes the southeast of the country and not London is the best barometer of housing market prices.
"If prices in the southeast rise by around 15 percent then I think the London effect will spread to the north, and we'd be seeing a stronger housing market across the nation," Marsh added.

With memories of the housing boom of the late 1980s still fresh in their minds, many analysts have voiced concerns that the UK is in for a repeat performance. The boom was dramatically replaced by a market collapse in the early 1990s that left many home-owners holding negative equity.

They are particularly concerned that windfall payments totalling 30 billion pounds from a string of building society flotations will combine with already growing earnings and income tax cuts to send house prices spiralling higher.
Some signs of inflationary pressure coming from the housing market are already apparent.

The Office of National Statistics on Thursday attributed an increase in May headline inflation to an increase in housing costs. Inflation rose 0.4 percent in May, pushing the year-on-year rate up to 2.6 percent from 2.4 percent in April.
The Bank of England has already raised interest rates twice since the new government took office on May 2 in order to keep inflationary pressure at bay.
But analysts said that this will not help the patchy housing market recovery since it will hit buyers everywhere.
Nor would the much-talked of abolition of mortgage interest tax relief (Miras), do much to rebalance the housing market recovery away from London and into the regions.

The current Miras structure is of greater benefit to homeowners in the more depressed areas of Britain where house prices are lower as it covers the first 30,000 pounds of a mortgage regardless of the total price.
Nikko's Briscoe thinks Miras should eventually be abolished, but the July budget would be the wrong time to do it.

"Economically and politically it's not the right time to abolish Miras, because the people at the low end of the property market, who benefit most from it, are not the ones currently enjoying Britain's boom," he said.
The Confederation of British Industry, a leading business lobby, this week also said it was opposed to an early abolition pf Miras.
Director General Adair Turner said he favoured a gradual change. "It would be undesirable to run the risk of reversing the less pronounced recovery in regions outside the South East," Turner said.
The government should not risk pushing homeowners back into negative equity, he added.
But increasing stamp duty on high-priced properties would help to narrow the north/south divide in Britain's property market, Briscoe said.

The Halifax forecasts house price growth will continue to advance, but not spiral, with prices averaging seven percent growth during 1997. Prices would hover between six and seven percent during 1998, it said.
